incumbent.name: Jennifer Meltzer
incumbent.summary: Jennifer Meltzer, a Shelbyville attorney and former deputy attorney general, has represented House District 73 since November 2022 {caucus_meltzer}{wiki_meltzer}. The House Republican caucus lists her as vice chair of the Courts and Criminal Code Committee {caucus_meltzer}.
record: Committees: Courts and Criminal Code (vice chair), Judiciary, and Local Government, per the caucus's member page {caucus_meltzer}.
2023: Her first law, HEA 1286, requires coroners to test for xylazine, a veterinary sedative found mixed into street drugs, in suspected overdose deaths {caucus_hea1286}.

2024: Authored HEA 1203, which made possessing xylazine without a prescription a crime and set penalties for dealing it, effective July 1, 2024 {caucus_hea1203}. She said the law was "a strong step in the right direction to help law enforcement get 'tranq' off of our streets" {caucus_hea1203}.

Voted yes on SEA 1, the 2025 property-tax law (April 10, 2025) {rc_sea1_433}, and yes on the 2025 budget conference report, HEA 1001 (April 25, 2025) {rc_hb1001_576}. Was one of the Republicans who voted no on HB 1032, the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which passed the House 57-41 on Dec. 5, 2025 {rc_hb1032_28}.

race_context: House District 73 covers portions of Bartholomew, Decatur, Jennings and Shelby counties in southeastern Indiana, per the House Republican caucus {caucus_meltzer}.
Meltzer is seeking a third full term; she won 76.9% of the vote in 2024 {wiki_2026}.
May 5, 2026 Republican primary: Meltzer 3,675 votes (66.6%), Edward Comstock 1,844 (33.4%) {wiki_2026}. A.J. Miller was the only Democratic candidate {wiki_2026}.

Key differences: Miller's campaign lists labor, infrastructure, education, natural resources, public health and legalizing cannabis as issues {miller_issues}; Meltzer's campaign site lists opposition to abortion, support for gun rights, school choice and reducing regulation {meltzer_site}.
No debate or forum for this race was found.

candidates.summary: A.J. Miller is a technical writer from Greensburg making his first run for office {miller_about}. He was the only Democrat in the May primary {wiki_2026}.
background: Works as a technical writer producing repair documentation, and says this is his first run for office {miller_about}.
Grew up on a small farm outside Pendleton; lives in Greensburg {miller_about}.
Lists membership in the Indiana Rural Summit {miller_site}.
path_to_ballot: Was the only Democratic candidate in the May 5, 2026 primary {wiki_2026}.

items: Says "Everyday Hoosiers continue to struggle while those in power benefit from our struggle" and that he would work to even the playing field {miller_issues}.
Calls for repairing existing infrastructure first and then pursuing long-term preventative solutions, with technology as part of that work {miller_issues}.
Supports better educational opportunities, more support for teachers and more support for the trades {miller_issues}.
Says natural resources should be prioritized and protected from excessive industrial development {miller_issues}.
Says he would pursue policies aimed at a healthier Indiana {miller_issues}. Supports legalizing and regulating cannabis, citing economic growth and health benefits {miller_issues}.

on_incumbent: Says he started the campaign "as a way to take a principled stand that no incumbent should run unopposed" {miller_site}. His campaign site does not mention Meltzer by name; he says lawmakers have ignored public testimony {miller_about}.
plans: Says he wants to bring "Better Outcomes for the State of Indiana" {miller_about}.
endorsements_finance: No endorsements are listed on his campaign site {miller_site}.
gaps: No news coverage of his campaign was found; local outlets The Republic and Shelby County news sites could not be read.
His campaign site does not give detailed stances on property taxes or the state budget.

candidates.summary: Jennifer Meltzer is the two-term incumbent, a Shelbyville attorney who represents the city of Shelbyville {caucus_meltzer}. She won the Republican primary with 66.6% {wiki_2026}.
background: Attorney who represents the city of Shelbyville; previously a deputy attorney general and an Indiana Department of Health employee {caucus_meltzer}.
Psychology degree from Xavier University and law degree from the IU McKinney School of Law {caucus_meltzer}.
path_to_ballot: Won the May 5, 2026 Republican primary over Edward Comstock, 66.6% to 33.4% {wiki_2026}.

items: Authored the 2023 and 2024 xylazine laws on overdose testing and criminal penalties {caucus_hea1286}{caucus_hea1203}.
Her campaign site describes her as "Pro-Life" {meltzer_site}.
Her campaign site describes her as "Pro 2nd Amendment" {meltzer_site}.
Campaign site lists "Empowering parents to choose the best education for their children" {meltzer_site}.
Voted no on the December 2025 congressional redistricting bill, HB 1032 {rc_hb1032_28}.

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. No statements about her challenger were found {meltzer_site}.
plans: Campaign site lists "Fighting unnecessary government regulation" {meltzer_site}.
endorsements_finance: Endorsed by Gov. Mike Braun, the NFIB Indiana PAC and the NRA Political Victory Fund, per Wikipedia's race listing {wiki_2026}.
gaps: No public statement explaining her no vote on HB 1032 was found.

Search snippets (unverified) say she authored HB 1312 (2025, public notices), which passed the House 57-36, and filed HB 1055 (December 2025) to let cities and towns move municipal elections to even-numbered years; final status not confirmed.
No 2025–2026 bills she authored were confirmed as enacted.
